newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thais fear devaluation will hit where it hurts most.
newsitem.headline: Thais fear devaluation will hit where it hurts most.

text.p: It may be good for the economy, but Thais are worried the defacto devaluation of the baht will hit where it hurts the most -- in the pocketbook.
Just a day after the currency was floated, Thais on Thursday were worrying about the impact on their own lives.

Lunchrooms, gyms and offices buzzed with people talking about how and where the 15-20 percent overnight drop in value was going to hurt. Hardest hit will probably be those most able to afford it -- people travelling abroad or buying imported, luxury goods.
But local prices jumped immediately and workers suddenly realised their salary was not worth as much as it was last week.
Amnuay Chanket, a 30-year-old maid, complained that the price of a traditional papaya salad called "somtam" had jumped 33 percent overnight even though it used no imported ingredients.
"For lower-paid people like me, the rise like this in the price of food like somtam, a staple, is not good news," she said.
Anuchit Nguyen, who is off to Britain for graduate work later this year, said he had lost about 60,000 baht ($2,142) because of the float.

"Just a couple of days ago I told the university to charge the last payment of 10,000 pounds to my credit card. When I told them the rate was about 43-44 baht to the pound, but now, by the time the bill goes through it will be 49-50. So I have to borrow about 60,000 baht more to be able to pay the bill," he said.

Expatriates and people preparing to travel abroad also complained of problems trying to buy foreign currency from banks which were slow to understand the new exchange rate. Others were worried about high bills once they returned.
The government took the sudden, drastic action in an effort to help bolster its sagging economy which has been hard hit by high interest rates, low exports and high imports.
Financial authorities have been urging Thais, enthusiastic shoppers at home and abroad, to help the economy by saving more and resisting buying expensive imported goods.
The latest move is another effort to try to stem the amount of baht flowing out of the country. ($1 = 28 baht)
